etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English min, myn, from Old English mīn, from Proto-West Germanic *mīn, from Proto-Germanic *mīnaz, from Proto-Indo-European *méynos.

Cognate with Saterland Frisian mien, West Frisian myn, Dutch mijn, Low German mien, German mein, Danish, Swedish and Norwegian min, Icelandic mín.

definitions.definition: Used predicatively.

quote.citation: 1905, E. M. Forster, Where Angels Fear to Tread , chapter 7:
quote.text: "Ah, but how beautiful (my baby boy) is! And he is mine, mine for ever. Even if he hates me he will be mine. He cannot help it, he is made out of me; I am his father."

definitions.definition: Used substantively, with an implied noun.
Used absolutely, set off from the sentence.
(informal) My house or home.
As double possessive.
That or those belonging to me.
Used attributively after the noun it modifies.

quote.citation: 1610–1611 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tempest”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene i]:
quote.text: […]  Flesh and blood, / You, brother mine, that entertain'd ambition, /  […]

definitions.definition: Used attributively before a vowel.

quote.citation: 1862 February, Julia Ward Howe, “The Battle Hymn of the Republic”, in The Atlantic Monthly, volume IX, number LII, page 10:
quote.text: Mine eyes have seen the glory of the coming of the Lord: /  […]

quote.citation: 1930 Winter, Packard Motor Car Company, The Packard Magazine, Volume 9, Number 2, page 6,
quote.text: Mine host, it seemed, did favors for everybody...

definitions.definition: (archaic) My; belonging to me.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English, from Old French mine, from Late Latin mina, from Gaulish (compare to Welsh mwyn, Irish mianach (“ore”)), from Proto-Celtic *meinis (“ore, metal”).

definitions.definition: An excavation from which ore or solid minerals are taken, especially one consisting of underground tunnels.
(figurative) Any source of wealth or resources.

quote.citation: 1962 December, “Beyond the Channel: U.S.S.R.: Train speeds still rising”, in Modern Railways, page 418:
quote.text: To those seeking information about train services on the Continent, Cook's Continental Guide is always a mine of accurate information.

definitions.definition: (military) A passage dug toward or underneath enemy lines, which is then packed with explosives.
(military) A device intended to explode when stepped upon or touched, or when approached by a ship, vehicle, or person.

quote.citation: 1940 May, “Overseas Railways: Icebound Denmark”, in Railway Magazine, page 302:
quote.text: Pack ice, at times mounting to a height of 35 ft., snow, fog, and floating mines all played their part in the disorganisation of railway services, and most of the train ferry services were completely suspended for a month or more; [...].

definitions.definition: (pyrotechnics) A type of firework that explodes on the ground, shooting sparks upward.
(entomology) The cavity made by a caterpillar while feeding inside a leaf.
(computing) A machine or network of machines used to extract units of a cryptocurrency.
(transitive, intransitive) To remove (rock or ore) from the ground.
To dig into, for ore or metal.

quote.citation: 1837, Andrew Ure, Dictionary of Arts, Manufactures and Mines:
quote.text: Lead veins have been traced  […]  but they have not been mined.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To sow mines (the explosive devices) in (an area).
(transitive) To damage (a vehicle or ship) with a mine (an explosive device).
(intransitive) To dig a tunnel or hole; to burrow in the earth.
To dig away, or otherwise remove, the substratum or foundation of; to lay a mine under; to sap; to undermine.

quote.citation: a. 1628 (date written), John Hayward, The Life, and Raigne of King Edward the Sixt, London:  […]  [Eliot’s Court Press, and J. Lichfield at Oxford?] for Iohn Partridge, […], published 1630, →OCLC:

1814 July 7, [Walter Scott], Waverley; or, ’Tis Sixty Years Since. […], volume (please specify |volume=I to III), Edinburgh:  […] James Ballantyne and Co. for Archibald Constable and Co.; London: Longman, Hurst, Rees, Orme, and Brown, →OCLC:
quote.text: Too lazy, perhaps, to cut [these immense trees] down, the spoilers  […]  had mined them, and placed a quantity of gunpowder in the cavity.

definitions.definition: (by extension, figurative) To ruin or destroy by slow degrees or secret means.
(by extension, figurative) To tap into.
(slang) To pick one's nose.
(cryptocurrencies) To earn new units of cryptocurrency by doing certain calculations.

quote.citation: 2021 March 9, Andrew Ross Sorkin, “Bitcoin's Climate Problem”, in The New York Times‎[1], →ISSN:
quote.text: Bitcoin supporters say that estimates of its carbon footprint are overstated. And if the computers that mine and help transact bitcoins are attached to an electric grid that uses wind and solar power, they add, mining and using it will become cleaner over time.

definitions.definition: Alternative form of mien
